(2) functional effect traits, which reflect how species influence ecosystem processes, community structure, or environmental conditions, often at broader spatial and temporal scales (Violle et al. 2007). Fountain-Jones et al. (2015) proposed a structured framework for analyzing functional traits in adult beetles, focusing on four trait types: morphological (e.g. body size, color, and wing length), physiological (e.g. food and microclimate preferences), phenological (e.g. breeding season and season of peak abundance), and ecological (e.g. habitat and feeding guild). This M–P–P–E framework provides a basis for linking beetle traits to both environmental drivers and ecosystem functions.

This study investigates the functional biodiversity of beetles and ants across four biotope types: (1) pine plantations, (2) new recovery (cleared 10 years ago), (3) old recovery (cleared 30 years ago), and (4) sites never planted, referred to as “pristine fynbos.” The main aim is to assess insect recovery following pine removal by analyzing functional richness, functional diversity, functional dispersion, RaoQ, and trait composition. Specifically, we address three objectives: to (1) determine which recovery stage most closely resembles pristine fynbos in terms of functional assemblages, (2) identify which functional traits respond to environmental changes driven by restoration, and (3) evaluate the potential of beetles and ants as bioindicators of restoration success post pine removal. We hypothesize that old recovery sites will be most functionally similar to pristine fynbos across all functional diversity indices, reflecting progressive recovery over time. We also predict that functional traits associated with dispersal will be more prevalent in recovery sites than in pristine fynbos, reflecting colonization dynamics, while traits linked to stable habitat conditions, such as larger body size, will be more common in pristine fynbos. Additionally, we expect herbivorous species to recolonize more rapidly than other feeding guilds due to increased resource availability from regenerating vegetation. Finally, we anticipate that beetles and ants will demonstrate recovery and that their functional trait responses will validate their use as indicator taxa for ecosystem restoration. This study contributes to the limited understanding of insect functional recovery following pine removal and passive restoration and provides insights to guide management in this globally important biodiversity hotspot.

We conducted this study in Table Mountain National Park (TMNP) bordered by the City of Cape Town, within the southwestern CFR. The CFR ranks among the world’s six floral kingdoms (Goldblatt 1997; Manning & Goldblatt 2012) and 35 global biodiversity hotspots, hosting approximately 9400 vascular plant species, 69% of which are endemic (Mittermeier et al. 2011). TMNP’s dominant vegetation is fynbos, a fireprone and fire-adapted shrubland with a Mediterranean-type climate of cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers. Fire records show that none of the sampled sites had burned since the 1960s. Thus, all treatments represent long-unburnt Peninsula Granite Fynbos, with differences reflecting time since pine removal rather than recent post-fire succession.

Figure 1. Left: A map showing the study area and the location of sites. Fyn, fynbos; OR, old recovering fynbos; NR, new recovering fynbos; Pine, pine plantations. Top right: study area shown with respect to South Africa. Bottom right: study area with respect to the Cape Peninsula.

Fountain-Jones et al. (2015) outline a comprehensive set of beetle traits relevant for assessing ecological responses to habitat change. From this suite, we selected four key traits for beetles: body size, dispersal power (calculated as leg length divided by body length), color variation, and feeding guild (Table S1). For ants, we focused on morphological traits linked to foraging and dispersal: body size, dispersal power (Almeida et al. 2023; Drager et al. 2023) and, given the ecological importance of habitat vertical stratification, nesting type (arboreal, leaf litter, and soil) (Vogel et al. 2024). We included additional morphological ant traits such as color variation, number of spines, pilosity, and cuticle sculpturing, following trait descriptions in the Global Ants Database. Feeding guild was excluded for ants since 20 of 21 species sampled were predators (with some opportunistic sap feeders), with only one herbivorous species found (Table S2). For each species, six individuals were measured and averaged (see Table 1).
